ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 4 — Annual Wellness Visit, Subsequent — Emile Griffith — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

text.paragraph: Emile Griffith is a 67-year-old retired boxer with mild cognitive impairment, most likely due to traumatic brain injury, and chronic PTSD, who comes with his care partner for his subsequent annual wellness visit, seven weeks after the diagnosis was explained to him. He has finished eleven of twelve sessions of cognitive processing therapy and takes sertraline 50 mg each morning without nausea, dizziness or bleeding. He says the nightmares about the fight come about twice a week now instead of most nights, and last week he read his own written account of the fight aloud to his psychologist. He uses one wall calendar and phone reminders, and has not been lost since he began sharing his phone location. Physical therapy for balance began six weeks ago, after a missed first appointment, and he has had no falls. He wants to settle who will speak for him while he can still decide it himself. [S]

Next scheduled visit 2005-09-15: four-month review: PTSD after cognitive processing therapy, mood, sodium, falls and caregiver strain. [S]

Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 30 minutes with him and his care partner, at his request, while he can take part fully. His capacity for these decisions was assessed: he understood what a health care agent does, explained in his own words why he chose his agent, and gave consistent answers. He signed a New York health care proxy naming his care partner as his health care agent, with a family member on the islands as the alternate; neither is named here. He said that what matters most is staying in his own home, being with the people he loves, being treated with respect, and not being a burden. If his memory one day fails to the point that he no longer knows the people close to him, he wants care focused on comfort, at home if possible, with no feeding tube and no machines to keep him alive; he wants his care partner and family to be able to visit and stay with him wherever he is. Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment were explained for a later stage and are not needed now. A financial power of attorney was discussed and he will arrange it. The plan will be revisited every year and at any change in his health. [S]
